newsitem.title: UK: Britain condemns nationalist violence in N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Britain condemns nationalist violence in N.Ireland.

text.p: Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, on Monday condemned "orchestrated violence" that swept through Irish nationalist communities in the province overnight in protest at a Protestant parade.

Mowlam was speaking after Northern Ireland's worst outbreak of nationalist unrest in years in which rioters and police clashed in Belfast, Londonderry and other towns after an Orange Order march through a Catholic area of Portadown.
Mowlam told a Belfast news conference: "I understand the anger there is in nationalist communities, but nothing justified the orchestrated violence that we have seen in the last 24 hours."
British Prime Minister Tony Blair backed his embattled Northern Ireland Secretary and pledged to press on with the search for peace through year-old Northern Ireland talks.
"We are going to go on searching for peace," Blair told reporters. "We will not give up, even for a moment."
Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern, whose government is co-sponsor with London of a fragile Northern Ireland peace process, said he would be holding more talks with Blair later on Monday.

"Like any violence it has to be condemened. The frustrations of nationalist people are I think understood but I would just far prefer to see all these matters dealt with and handled in a peaceful way," Ahern told reporters.
The IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, meanwhile called for "calm and dignified" protests, saying the rioting was counterproductive.
Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams said: "We want to call for an end to the hijackings and burnings."

In her first comments on the violence, Mowlam called on the Protestant Orange Order to display "willingness and understanding" in the holding of parades as their annual "marching season" reaches its high point this week.
"There can and should be no triumphalism," she said.
Mowlam backed a decision by police chiefs to allow the Orange Order to hold their annual parade along the Garvaghy Road area of Portadown on Sunday over the objections of Roman Catholic residents.

She said she had tried an failed to reach a compromise with Catholic residents of Garvaghy Road and with the Orange marchers. She would be holding more talks with both Catholics and Protestants in the hope of averting more violence.

The display of firepower by the Irish Republican Army in overnight unrest across the province was the biggest in years and the outpouring of nationalist fury appeared to mark the end of any honeymoon with Britain's new Labour government.
A bomb was thrown at a Belfast police station and a 14-year-old boy was in critical condition in hospital after being hit on the head by a plastic bullet.
Another 14-year-old boy suffered gunshot wounds to the shoulder. Dozens more were injured as the unrest spread.
Sinn Fein denied it was responsible for provoking the unrest despite comments by one of its senior figures urging Catholics to take to the streets,

"The events that we saw over the past 24 hours were provoked by the shameful decision of the British government to capitulate to the Orange Order's demands to march through nationalist areas where there is fear and trepidation at their presence," Sinn Fein chairman Mitchel McLaughlin said.
David Trimble, leader of the pro-British Ulster Unionist Party, said the IRA had been planning violence.
"I think that came out very clearly last night, with the clearly prepared reaction that the IRA orchestrated throughout Northern Ireland.
Ian Paisley, leader of the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, added: "The last days...have indicated just what the IRA are after -- a complete reign of anarchy."
The IRA, which enjoys support among some sections of the 40 per cent Catholic minority, is fighting a 28-year war to end British rule of Northern Ireland.
